Those arrests captured important members of a powerful Sicilian clan linked to Mafia boss Salvatore Lo Piccolo, who was believed to be the successor to the “boss of bosses,” Bernardo Provenzano.

Police say that, in his attempt to rise to power, Lo Piccolo tried to mend ties with New York-based Mafia families after those relationships were broken during the bloody Mafia wars of the 1980s. Those families included the Gambinos of New York and the Inzerillos of Italy.

But there was certainly an attempt to re-establish that connection.”

Investigators believe mob clans wanted to collaborate on illegal commercial ventures, including money laundering and drug trafficking. NEW YORK (CNN) — Prosecutors said Thursday that a sweeping anti-Mafia operation reaching from New York to Sicily had done far more than remove the leadership of the Gambino crime family, saying it had also taken out much of the organization’s upper structure.

John “Jackie the Nose” D’Amico, pictured in 1992, was among 62 people indicted. Those charged are alleged members of the Gambino, Genovese and Bonanno crime families and face a total of 80 counts, including money laundering, illegal gambling and murder.

“These charges strike at the very core of the Gambino family,” said Benton Campbell, the U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of New York.

According to the indictment, the Gambino family made money through extortion connected to New York’s construction business and labor unions. Gordon Heddell, inspector general of the U.S. Department of Labor, said several businesses allegedly paid a “mob tax” in exchange for “protection” and “permission to operate.”

Other accusations center on an illegal gambling operation, Queens County District Attorney Richard Brown said. Brown alleged that Nicholas Corozzo, described as a Gambino captain, took part in a sports-betting business that used toll-free phone lines as part of its operation.

The indictment also charges four Gambino family members with eight offenses tied to murder. Among them is the felony murder of Jose Delgado Rivera, who was shot to death inside an armored truck during a 1990 robbery.

“Today we are able to bring closure to crimes from the past that have never been forgotten,” Campbell said, adding that the alleged crimes go back more than 30 years.

A central element in Thursday’s Gambino arrests was an undercover member of the attorney general’s Organized Crime Task Force, who penetrated the Gambino organization and secretly recorded hundreds of hours of conversations, according to John Milgrim, a spokesman for the attorney general.

Police said 45 of the defendants were already in custody. Arrests took place in New York City, on Long Island, and in New Jersey.

New York Attorney General Andrew Cuomo compared organized crime to weeds growing through cracks in society, calling it persistent and difficult to eradicate. “We will not rest until organized crime is a distant memory,” he said.

Alongside the arrests in the New York region, Italian police detained 77 people in an organized-crime investigation. Those arrests included prominent figures from a powerful Sicilian clan connected to Mafia boss Salvatore Lo Piccolo, who was believed to be the likely successor to Bernardo Provenzano, the so-called “boss of bosses.”

Authorities said Lo Piccolo, in his effort to gain power, tried to repair relations with Mafia families based in New York after those connections were damaged during the violent Mafia conflicts of the 1980s. Those families included New York’s Gambinos and Italy’s Inzerillos. Provenzano was captured two years earlier in Corleone.

Francesco Messineo of the Italian police said it was clear that Palermo’s Mafia wanted to reopen communication with the United States through the Inzerillo family. He noted that ties between American and Italian Mafia groups were longstanding and rooted in tradition, but said there was a definite effort to renew that relationship.

Investigators believe the Mafia groups hoped to work together on illegal business activities, including money laundering and drug trafficking. Italian authorities said the arrests were intended to stop those crimes before they occurred. They also warned, however, that other Sicilian Mafia clans opposed the Inzerillo family’s return to the island, raising fears of another Mafia war.

CNN’s Deborah Feyerick and Alessio Vinci contributed to the report.
